comment: COMP1511 is a fundamental introductory compulsory course for computer science majors at UNSW, primarily teaching C programming, basic algorithmic concepts, and simple program design methodologies. The overall pace of the course is relatively intense (9 weeks + flex), but the content is arranged progressively from simple to more advanced (from the most basic C syntax to slightly more complex data structures like structs and linked lists). It is suitable for students with little programming background to build a foundation, but those with absolutely no prior experience may feel some pressure in the mid-to-late stages of the semester. The strength of this course lies in its strong practical focus; labs, assignments, and autotests help students quickly develop the mindset of "writing code — debugging — improving." Although the content is introductory, it places considerable emphasis on programming standards, logical expression, and problem decomposition, so the improvement after completing the course is quite noticeable. It also cultivates the habit of writing comments, laying the groundwork for subsequent courses, group collaboration, and code maintenance. The difficulty lies in the fact that concepts may seem few early on, but once students move into arrays, functions, pointers, structs, linked lists, and more complex program design, many begin to struggle. If students only attend lectures without hands-on practice, it's easy to fall behind later. The importance of regular lab exercises becomes evident here. Meanwhile, assignments provide students with an opportunity to complete a small project over a longer period (2–3 weeks), accounting for about 30%–40% of the course grade. The assignment guide breaks the entire project into several smaller parts, guiding students step-by-step to complete the main portion (usually around 80%; the remaining parts may involve content from later courses and are intended for students with some programming ability or those aiming for grades of 75+ or 85+). Students can selectively complete assignment tasks based on their own capabilities and the grade distribution. Finally, the exam typically accounts for 40%–50% of the course grade and consists of around 10 programming questions covering almost all data structures and functions learned throughout the semester. Generally, students are required to complete at least 40% of the exam content (a hurdle, which may include specific questions). One question might test a single data structure, while subsequent questions may involve the application of two or more data structures within a single problem. The last one or two questions may involve content from later courses and are intended for students with some programming ability or those aiming for grades of 75+ or 85+. Overall, COMP1511 is a foundational and highly valuable course for training. It not only teaches C syntax but, more importantly, helps establish the fundamental mindset of computer science. It is crucial for subsequent studies in data structures, algorithms, and systems-related courses.

COMP4920 is a course focused on professional ethics and technology ethics, with an emphasis not on programming implementation but on discussing ethical judgment, sense of responsibility in the computer profession, and the social impact of technology applications. This course covers ethical theories, moral judgment, and the application of these frameworks to analyze real-world computer science cases. The course is characterized by its strong emphasis on critical thinking, as well as high requirements for writing and argumentation. It is particularly suitable for students who have already taken multiple technical courses and wish to move beyond "how to build systems" to consider "why we build them this way and whether this approach is responsible." Its value lies not in improving coding skills but in helping students develop a more comprehensive professional perspective.

Overall, COMP4920 is more like a course that helps computer science students fill in the gaps in professional ethics and critical thinking. For students aiming to enter the software, AI, or broader technology industries, it encourages a shift from focusing solely on technical implementation to considering the responsibilities and impacts behind technological decisions.

Now, moving from the technical summary to personal feelings: This course primarily covers computer ethics and morality. It doesn’t require any coding, but students must write two essays and deliver a final presentation. Students need to choose topics and read academic materials provided by the instructor or find relevant sources online to support their arguments. The process is extremely painful and particularly torturous for students with little interest in this area. If the tutor has a non-computer science background (e.g., in philosophy), it can be even more torturous. Non-computer science tutors may provide "less accurate" guidance or assistance when topics or questions fall outside their area of expertise (such as specialized computer science knowledge). They might also scrutinize your essays from their own professional perspective and way of thinking, which can be extremely challenging for students who haven’t systematically developed their logical and critical thinking skills. Additionally, the grading is very stingy and subjective. If the tutor is competent, your grade won’t be too bad, but if the tutor is incompetent, you’re basically doomed.

The course arrangement for COMP2521 is meticulously designed, with specific themes and learning objectives each week. The course helps students comprehensively grasp knowledge of data structures and algorithms through various formats such as lectures, videos, lab exercises, quizzes, and assignments.  
Week 1: Introduction and Recursion  
Theme: Course introduction, recursion concepts, algorithm analysis.  
Resources: Video lectures, YouTube videos, code examples.  
Week 2: Sorting Algorithms  
Theme: Introduction to sorting algorithms, basic sorting, divide-and-conquer sorting, non-comparison sorting.  
Resources: Multiple video lectures, YouTube videos, code, and visualization tools.  
Week 3: Abstract Data Types  
Theme: Binary Search Trees.  
Resources: Video lectures, YouTube videos, code, and visualization tools.  
Week 4: Balanced Binary Trees  
Theme: Balanced binary trees, AVL trees.  
Resources: Video lectures, YouTube videos, code, and visualization tools.  
Week 5: Graph Basics and Traversal  
Theme: Basic concepts of graphs, graph traversal algorithms.  
Resources: Video lectures, YouTube videos, code, and visualization tools.  
Week 6: Flexible Learning Week  
Provides additional time for students to review and delve deeper into the material.  
Week 7: Directed Graph Algorithms  
Theme: Dijkstra's algorithm, minimum spanning trees.  
Resources: Video lectures, YouTube videos, code, and visualization tools.  
Week 8: Hash Tables  
Theme: Hash tables, applications of hash tables.  
Resources: Video lectures, YouTube videos, code, and visualization tools.  
Week 9: Priority Queues, Heaps, and Tries  
Theme: Priority queues, heaps, Trie trees.  
Resources: Video lectures, YouTube videos, code, and visualization tools.  
Week 10: Course Review and Exam  
Review the entire semester's content to prepare for the final exam.  
🎯 Learning Outcomes  
Through studying COMP2521, you will be able to:  
Analyze and measure algorithm performance.  
Select and develop appropriate data structures and algorithms for given problems.  
Reason about the effectiveness of data structures and algorithms.  
Package data structures and algorithms as abstract data types.  
Develop complex software systems using the C language.

I took 9301 and 9302 back-to-back, which essentially means doing one project over two semesters, leaning toward research. The good part is the high degree of freedom—you can choose your own direction, and if you’re genuinely interested in networking, you can actually learn a lot. But the downsides are also pretty obvious: first, the bar is really high, with a bunch of prerequisite courses; without planning ahead, it’s basically impossible to get in. Second, spots are very limited—in my year, it was basically a scramble; if you were even a little late, you’d miss out. Lastly, progress relies entirely on self-discipline; no one is constantly checking on you, so if you’re not self-motivated, it’s really easy to procrastinate until everything falls apart at the end. Overall, it doesn’t feel like “taking a course” as much as being thrown into doing a mini research project on your own. If you’re just looking to coast for credits, it’ll really be a pain.

If you’re already set on going into research or planning to apply for a PhD, this track can be quite useful. But if you’re just looking to take courses for credits, I really wouldn’t recommend touching this set.
